input.title: The Prague Spring Action Program and the Soviet-Led Response of August 1968

prompt.scenario: In the period c. 1956-1989, leaders in Soviet-bloc states tried to reform communist rule while staying within the limits Moscow would accept. In Czechoslovakia in 1968, a reform program adopted by the Communist Party (KSC) was ended by a military intervention led by the Soviet Union.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE way the excerpt indicates that the reformers of 1968 meant to keep their changes within the limits of communist rule.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific historical development in Czechoslovakia or the Soviet bloc between 1956 and August 1968 that helps explain why reformers in Czechoslovakia pursued changes like those described in the excerpt. Do not use the Action Program or the New Economic Model themselves as your answer.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific effect of the Soviet-led military intervention in Czechoslovakia in August 1968, either within Czechoslovakia or elsewhere in Europe, in the period 1968-1989.

requirements: Each part asks for ONE specific, historically accurate response.
Part B must name a development from 1956 to August 1968 that is not the Action Program or the New Economic Model.
Part C must name an effect from 1968 to 1989 and stay on Czechoslovakia or the European reaction to the intervention; responses about the Hungarian uprising of 1956 do not earn the point.

rows.task_specific: The response describes a feature of the excerpt that shows the reforms were meant to stay inside communist rule, for example that the program reaffirmed the alliance with the Soviet Union and other socialist states, kept communism as the goal while rejecting only Stalinism, or required that reform go forward under KSC direction.

descriptors.0: The response does not describe a limit stated in the excerpt, only lists reforms such as free expression, or makes a claim the excerpt does not support.
descriptors.1: The response accurately describes one way the excerpt shows the reforms were to stay within communist rule, such as the reaffirmed Soviet alliance, the continued goal of communism, or KSC direction of reform.

rows.task_specific: The response explains a specific development from 1956 to August 1968 that helps explain the push for reform, such as de-Stalinization after Khrushchev's 1956 speech, economic slowdown in Czechoslovakia in the early 1960s, the replacement of Antonin Novotny by Alexander Dubcek in January 1968, Slovak resentment of centralized rule, or the lifting of press censorship and the growth of public debate in spring 1968.

descriptors.0: The response names no relevant development, falls outside 1956 to August 1968, uses only the Action Program or New Economic Model, or explains nothing about why it encouraged reform.
descriptors.1: The response explains one accurate, specific development from 1956 to August 1968 and links it to the reform effort in Czechoslovakia.

rows.task_specific: The response explains a specific effect of the August 1968 intervention between 1968 and 1989, such as the Brezhnev Doctrine, Dubcek's removal and Husak's normalization, purges and renewed censorship, protests such as Jan Palach's self-immolation in January 1969, criticism from Romania or Western communist parties, or later dissent such as Charter 77.

descriptors.0: The response gives no accurate effect, describes the invasion itself without an effect, falls outside 1968 to 1989, or discusses Hungary in 1956 instead.
descriptors.1: The response explains one accurate, specific effect of the August 1968 intervention within Czechoslovakia or elsewhere in Europe between 1968 and 1989.

scoring_notes: ALTON reference — not official AP scoring
Each part is scored on its own; a point earned in one part does not depend on any other part.
In Part A, listing reforms such as freedom of assembly or federalization does not earn the point unless the response ties them to a stated limit, such as KSC direction or the Soviet alliance.
In Part B, naming Dubcek alone does not earn the point; the response must point to a development, such as his replacing Novotny in January 1968, and show how it opened the way to reform.
In Part C, federalization taking effect on 1 January 1969 can earn the point if the response explains that it was the main reform to survive after the intervention.
Brief responses can earn each point if they are specific and accurate; responses need not be full paragraphs.

facts: Alexander Dubcek replaced Antonin Novotny as First Secretary of the Czechoslovak Communist Party in January 1968.
The KSC Presidium adopted the Action Program in April 1968.
Press censorship was relaxed and then lifted during spring 1968, and open public debate grew.
The Two Thousand Words manifesto, written by Ludvik Vaculik, was published in June 1968 and called for faster reform.
On the night of 20-21 August 1968, troops from the Soviet Union and several Warsaw Pact allies invaded Czechoslovakia.
Romania refused to take part in the intervention, and its leader Nicolae Ceausescu condemned it publicly.
Czechoslovak leaders were taken to Moscow and signed the Moscow Protocol in August 1968, which committed them to roll back reforms.
The Brezhnev Doctrine, stated in autumn 1968, claimed the right of socialist states to intervene when socialism was threatened in another socialist state.
The student Jan Palach set himself on fire in Prague in January 1969 to protest the occupation and the loss of reforms.
Gustav Husak replaced Dubcek as party leader in April 1969 and led the policy known as normalization.
Federalization took effect on 1 January 1969, creating Czech and Slovak socialist republics within Czechoslovakia.
Charter 77, a human rights declaration whose spokesmen included Vaclav Havel, appeared in January 1977.
Khrushchev's 1956 speech criticizing Stalin started de-Stalinization across the Soviet bloc.

a: The excerpt says the Action Program reaffirmed Czechoslovakia's alliance with the Soviet Union and other socialist states, which shows the reformers did not plan to leave the Soviet bloc.
The excerpt says the reform movement rejected Stalinism but remained committed to communism as a goal, so it aimed to change methods rather than abandon communism.
The excerpt says the Action Program stipulated that reform must proceed under KSC direction, so the Communist Party would keep control of the process.
The excerpt calls the program a new model of socialism, which presents the changes as a version of socialism adapted to Czechoslovak conditions rather than a break with it.
b: De-Stalinization after Khrushchev's 1956 speech criticizing Stalin weakened the authority of hard-line leaders and encouraged communists in Czechoslovakia to imagine a less repressive socialism.
Slow economic growth in Czechoslovakia in the early 1960s discredited rigid central planning and led economists such as Ota Sik to argue for market-based reforms.
In January 1968 reform-minded party members replaced Antonin Novotny with Alexander Dubcek as First Secretary, giving reformers control of party leadership.
Many Slovaks resented centralized rule from Prague, and that pressure helps explain why the reform program called for federalizing the country.
When censorship was lifted in spring 1968, open discussion in the press and new citizens' clubs spread public demands for wider freedoms.
c: The intervention led to the Brezhnev Doctrine, which claimed a right for the Soviet bloc to intervene in any socialist state where socialism seemed threatened and shaped bloc politics until the late 1980s.
Dubcek was removed in April 1969 and replaced by Gustav Husak, whose normalization brought purges of reformers from the party, renewed censorship and an end to most of the Prague Spring reforms.
Jan Palach set himself on fire in January 1969 to protest the occupation, which made him a lasting symbol of resistance in Czechoslovakia.
Romania condemned the invasion and Western communist parties such as the Italian Communist Party criticized it, deepening divisions in European communism.
The failure of reform from within the party led later dissidents such as the authors of Charter 77 in 1977 to frame opposition in terms of human rights rather than reforming the party.

common_pitfalls: In Part A, listing the reforms (freedom of expression, democratized elections) without showing how the excerpt limits them.
In Part B, repeating the excerpt's own examples (the Action Program or New Economic Model) instead of a separate development.
In Part C, describing the 1956 Hungarian uprising or treating the invasion itself as the effect.
Claiming the reformers planned to leave the Warsaw Pact or restore capitalism, which the excerpt contradicts.
Dating the Brezhnev Doctrine or the Husak leadership before August 1968.
Treating the excerpt, a 1980s U.S. government reference book, as a 1968 primary source.
contextualization_ideas: Earlier de-Stalinization and attempts to reform the planned economy in the Soviet bloc.
Cold War bloc discipline enforced through the Warsaw Pact.

doc_uses.usable_for: Part A: identifying the program's stated limits (Soviet alliance, communist goal, KSC direction) and its proposed reforms.
doc_uses.sourcing: A secondary reference work prepared by the Federal Research Division of the Library of Congress for the U.S. government, with research completed in 1987, written during the Cold War, almost two decades after the events.

input.title: Peace, Security, or National Advantage? European Diplomatic Agreements, 1881 to 1925

prompt.scenario: Between the Three Emperors' League of 1881 and the Locarno agreements of 1925, European governments signed many treaties, conventions and alliances. Some promised to localize conflicts or guarantee frontiers. Others committed armies to mobilize, divided regions into spheres of influence, or assigned responsibility for a war. The seven documents include treaty texts signed by the great powers, a painting of the 1919 signing at Versailles by a British official war artist, and the memoirs of the former German emperor.
prompt.task: Evaluate the extent to which diplomatic agreements among European powers between 1881 and 1925 were aimed at preserving peace and security rather than at advancing the interests of individual states.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least four documents.
Use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence (beyond that found in the documents) relevant to an argument about the prompt.
For at least two documents, explain how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to an argument.
Demonstrate a complex understanding of the historical development that is the focus of the prompt, using evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument that addresses the question.

rows.task_specific: The thesis has to take a position on how far the agreements from 1881 to 1925 aimed at peace and security versus the interests of individual states, and it has to give a reason that organizes the essay. Examples: alliances that were defensive in wording served each state's security against particular rivals; or there was a shift from bloc-building before 1914 to collective guarantees at Locarno.

descriptors.0: Gives no defensible claim, only restates the prompt, or does not weigh peace and security against state interests.
descriptors.1: Makes a defensible claim about the extent to which the agreements aimed at peace and security rather than state interests, with a line of reasoning, in the introduction or conclusion.

rows.task_specific: Places the agreements in a broader setting, such as the European balance of power after German unification in 1871 and the Congress of Berlin, the imperial competition of the New Imperialism, the arms race and growing alliance blocs, or the destruction of the First World War and the instability of the early 1920s.

descriptors.0: Gives no relevant context, or only mentions a phrase or date without explaining it.
descriptors.1: Describes a broader development before, during or after 1881 to 1925 and connects it to the argument about the purposes of the agreements.

rows.task_specific: Uses what the documents actually say: the localization and Balkan clauses of the 1881 treaty, the mobilization commitments of 1892, the line dividing concessions in Persia, Articles 231 and 232, the Versailles setting in Orpen's painting, Wilhelm II's account of German economic rise, and the Locarno frontier guarantee and non-aggression pledge.

descriptors.0: Uses fewer than three documents accurately, or only quotes them without connecting them to the topic.
descriptors.1: Accurately describes the content of at least three documents and relates them to the topic.
descriptors.2: Uses the content of at least four documents to support an argument about the extent to which the agreements aimed at peace and security rather than state interests.

rows.task_specific: Gives at least one accurate, specific piece of evidence that is not in the documents and uses it in the argument. Examples: the Dual Alliance of 1879, the Triple Alliance of 1882, the Reinsurance Treaty of 1887 and its lapse in 1890, the Entente Cordiale of 1904, the Moroccan crises, the Bosnian crisis of 1908, the League of Nations, the Ruhr occupation of 1923, the Dawes Plan of 1924.

descriptors.0: Gives no outside evidence, or the evidence is inaccurate or merely named.
descriptors.1: Uses at least one specific, accurate piece of outside evidence to support an argument about the purposes of the agreements.

rows.task_specific: For at least two documents, explains how the point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience affects their use in the argument. Examples: the treaties of 1881 and 1892 were secret, the 1892 convention was drafted by general staffs, Orpen was a British official war artist, Wilhelm II wrote in exile after abdicating, and Locarno was a public agreement that included defeated Germany.

descriptors.0: Gives no sourcing, or only restates the credit line without explaining why it matters.
descriptors.1: For at least two documents, explains how point of view, purpose, historical situation or audience matters to the argument.

rows.task_specific: Shows a complex understanding. Examples: treating peace and state interest as overlapping rather than opposite, since defensive alliances and spheres of influence lowered some tensions and sharpened others; explaining change over time from secret bloc treaties to public collective guarantees; or corroborating and qualifying claims across several documents and sources.

descriptors.0: Gives no complex understanding, or only mentions complexity in a phrase.
descriptors.1: Shows complex understanding through sustained analysis, such as weighing multiple causes or purposes, explaining change and continuity, or using the documents to qualify the argument.

scoring_notes: ALTON reference — not official AP scoring
Document 6 is a memoir, not an agreement; credit students who use it as evidence of the rivalries and national ambitions behind the agreements, or of the German reaction to Article 231.

For Document 5, accept only claims supported by what is visible or by the context line: the Hall of Mirrors setting, the gilded decoration, the inscription beginning 'Le roy gouverne', the delegates gathered around a table, and the signing. Do not require students to identify individual delegates.
Students may argue either that the agreements mainly served peace or that they mainly served state interests. A thesis that shows these overlapped or changed over time is also defensible.
Outside evidence used for contextualization cannot also earn the outside evidence point unless it is a separate piece of evidence.

defensible_theses: Most agreements from 1881 to 1914 were written in the language of peace, but each one mainly served a signatory's security against particular rivals or its imperial ambitions. The 1881 promise to localize conflicts, the 1892 mobilization pledge and the 1907 division of Persia protected individual states and hardened rival blocs. After the war, the Versailles settlement imposed the victors' interests, and Locarno in 1925 was a limited move toward collective guarantees.

The aims of these agreements changed over time. Bismarck's alliances of the 1880s tried to keep the peace by isolating France and managing Austro-Russian rivalry in the Balkans. The military and imperial agreements of the 1890s and 1900s put national advantage and readiness for war first. The Locarno Pact turned back toward mutual security by having former enemies guarantee frontiers together.

Peace and state interest were not opposites, because great powers thought their own security was the same thing as peace. Each agreement promoted peace for some states by preparing for war or imposing terms on others. That is why the 1892 convention, Article 231 and even Locarno, which guaranteed only Germany's western borders, lowered some tensions and created others.
contextualization_ideas: After German unification in 1871 and the proclamation of the German Empire at Versailles, Bismarck tried to isolate France and keep Austria-Hungary and Russia from fighting over the Balkans. The Congress of Berlin in 1878 had left Austro-Russian rivalry there unresolved.

The New Imperialism of the late nineteenth century, including the Scramble for Africa and competition in Central Asia (the Great Game between Britain and Russia), made great-power agreements partly about colonial spheres and markets.

The First World War caused enormous loss of life, the collapse of the German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman empires, and economic disruption. This shaped the Paris Peace Conference, the founding of the League of Nations, and the crises of the early 1920s such as the Ruhr occupation.
outside_evidence: The Dual Alliance of 1879 between Germany and Austria-Hungary, and the Triple Alliance of 1882, which added Italy.
The Reinsurance Treaty of 1887 between Germany and Russia, which Germany did not renew in 1890 after Bismarck's dismissal. This opened the way for Franco-Russian cooperation.
The Entente Cordiale of 1904 between Britain and France settled colonial disputes, including recognition of British interests in Egypt and French interests in Morocco.
The First Moroccan Crisis and the Algeciras Conference of 1906, and the Second Moroccan Crisis of 1911, tested the alliance blocs.
The Bosnian annexation crisis of 1908, when Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina, angered Serbia and Russia.
The Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885 set rules for European claims in Africa.
Wilson's Fourteen Points and the Covenant of the League of Nations proposed collective security after the war.
The French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr in 1923 and the Dawes Plan of 1924, which rescheduled German reparation payments.
Germany entered the League of Nations in 1926 after Locarno. Briand and Stresemann received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926.

doc_uses.usable_for: Peace aims: benevolent neutrality and efforts toward the 'localization of the conflict', plus a pledge to avoid 'discord' in the Balkans. State interest: it protects Austria-Hungary's position under the Treaty of Berlin and each court's 'respective interests'.
doc_uses.sourcing: It was a secret treaty among three monarchies, so it was meant for the governments themselves, not the public. It shows the powers managing their own Balkan rivalry while promising neutrality only to each other, not to Europe as a whole.

doc_uses.usable_for: State interest and the forming of blocs: France and Russia each pledge 'all her available forces' against Germany and promise immediate mobilization if the Triple Alliance mobilizes. This can be read as defensive security or as preparation for war.
doc_uses.sourcing: Army officers of the two general staffs signed it in secret. Its purpose was military planning, which explains its focus on mobilization and moving troops to the frontiers rather than on settling disputes.

doc_uses.usable_for: State interest through imperial spheres: Britain agrees not to seek railway, bank or other concessions beyond a fixed line and not to oppose Russian-backed concessions there. It also shows tension between the two powers being eased.
doc_uses.sourcing: Two great powers made the agreement about territory belonging to a third country. The historical situation of imperial rivalry in Asia matters, because Persia was not a signatory. The excerpt gives only the British commitments.

doc_uses.usable_for: State interest and victors' security: Article 231 has Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage of a war 'imposed' by German aggression. Article 232 admits that Germany's resources cannot make complete reparation.
doc_uses.sourcing: It is a peace treaty between victors and a defeated Germany. The situation after a costly war explains why the wording assigns responsibility to Germany and its allies and works to secure compensation for the Allied side.

doc_uses.usable_for: The Versailles settlement as a ceremony of victory: the signing takes place in the gilded Hall of Mirrors under an inscription beginning 'Le roy gouverne', and the delegates are small beneath the grand architecture. It can be used for the idea of a peace imposed with symbols of power.
doc_uses.sourcing: Orpen was a British official war artist, so his view comes from the victors' side. The setting itself matters: the Hall of Mirrors was where the German Empire had been proclaimed in 1871.

doc_uses.usable_for: The national ambitions and rivalries behind the pre-war agreements: Wilhelm II describes Germany's 'peaceful penetration' of world markets as something 'disagreeable' to older nations, especially England. It can also be used for German rejection of the responsibility assigned in Article 231.
doc_uses.sourcing: The former emperor wrote this in exile after abdicating, in a chapter on the question of guilt. His purpose of defending his own reign and his country affects how reliable his account is.

doc_uses.usable_for: Peace and collective security: the parties 'collectively and severally guarantee' the western frontiers and the demilitarized zone, and Germany, France and Belgium promise not to attack each other. It can also be read as confirming the Versailles settlement in the interest of France and Belgium.
doc_uses.sourcing: Unlike the secret treaties of 1881 and 1892, this agreement included defeated Germany as an equal party. The situation after the Ruhr crisis matters. It covers only the frontiers of Germany with France and Belgium.

evidence_map.line: Agreements aimed at preserving peace by localizing conflicts and guaranteeing frontiers
Agreements mainly advanced the strategic, imperial or economic interests of individual states
Defensive security for some states produced rival blocs and insecurity for others
The postwar settlement moved from a victors' peace toward mutual guarantees

common_pitfalls: Treating Document 6 as a diplomatic agreement instead of a memoir that shows one side's account of the rivalries.
Saying the alliance system alone caused the First World War, instead of treating the alliances as one factor among several.
Describing details in Orpen's painting that are not visible, or naming individual delegates without support.
Calling Article 231 the 'war guilt clause' as if that were the treaty's own wording, or ignoring Article 232's admission about Germany's limited resources.
Arguing that Locarno guaranteed all of Germany's borders, when it covered only the frontiers with France and Belgium.
Summarizing the documents one by one without weighing peace against state interest.
facts: The Three Emperors' League was signed in June 1881, renewed in 1884, and lapsed in 1887.
The Franco-Russian military convention of 1892 became an alliance when it was ratified in 1894.
The Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 dealt with Persia, Afghanistan and Tibet.
The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors, where the German Empire had been proclaimed in January 1871.
The Locarno treaties were initialed in October 1925 and signed in London in December 1925.
Wilhelm II abdicated in November 1918 and went into exile in the Netherlands.

input.title: Kant on Standing Armies and the Wars of 1789-1815

prompt.scenario: In the period c. 1789-1815, European thinkers and governments argued over what caused war and how states might keep the peace. In 1795 the Prussian philosopher Immanuel Kant published Perpetual Peace, a proposal for ending war between states.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE argument Kant makes in the excerpt about why standing armies are harmful.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific military or political development in Europe between 1789 and 1815 that supports or challenges Kant's argument about standing armies. Do not use a development named in the excerpt.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE way the peace settlement that European powers made in 1814-1815 was similar to OR different from the approach to peace Kant proposes in the excerpt.

requirements: Each part is answered in a few sentences and earns at most one point.
Parts B and C must use specific historical evidence from 1789-1815.
Responses need not use complete essays; a thesis is not required.

rows.task_specific: Describe one argument from the excerpt: armies threaten other states by constant readiness; they cause arms races with no limit; their cost makes peace more oppressive than a short war, so states start aggressive wars to escape the burden; hiring soldiers treats people as machines or instruments of the state, against the right of humanity.

descriptors.0: The response does not accurately describe an argument in the excerpt, or only restates that armies are bad without a reason drawn from the text.
descriptors.1: The response accurately describes one specific reason Kant gives for why standing armies are harmful.

rows.task_specific: Explain one specific development from 1789-1815 (such as the levee en masse, Napoleonic conscription and the Grande Armee, the Prussian military reforms after Jena, the cost of war and the Continental System, or the Peace of Basel) and connect it to Kant's claim that large armies drive rivalry, burden states or lead to aggressive war, or show where events complicate his view.

descriptors.0: The response names no accurate development from 1789-1815, repeats the excerpt, or does not link the development to Kant's argument.
descriptors.1: The response explains one accurate, specific development from 1789-1815 and how it supports or challenges Kant's argument about standing armies.

rows.task_specific: Explain one similarity or difference between the 1814-1815 settlement (Treaties of Paris, Congress of Vienna, Quadruple Alliance, Holy Alliance, Concert of Europe) and Kant's approach. Differences: Vienna relied on a balance of power among great powers that kept large armies, restored monarchs on legitimacy, and redrew borders by great-power bargaining. Similarities: both sought a lasting peace through agreements among states and regular cooperation instead of constant war.

descriptors.0: The response does not accurately describe the 1814-1815 settlement or does not make a similarity or difference with Kant's approach clear.
descriptors.1: The response accurately explains one specific similarity or difference between the 1814-1815 settlement and the approach to peace in the excerpt.

scoring_notes: ALTON reference — not official AP scoring
Each part is scored on its own; a strong answer to one part cannot make up for a missing part.
For part B, either supporting or challenging evidence earns the point if the link to the excerpt is explained.
For part C, a response that only describes the Congress of Vienna without relating it to Kant's proposal does not earn the point.
Do not award credit for the partitions of Poland or for events outside 1789-1815 in parts B and C.

facts: Immanuel Kant taught at the University of Konigsberg in Prussia and published Perpetual Peace in 1795.
In 1795 Prussia made a separate peace with revolutionary France, the Peace of Basel, and left the war against France.
In August 1793 the French National Convention decreed the levee en masse, a mass mobilization of French men for the war.
Under Napoleon, conscription supplied the very large armies used in campaigns across Europe, including the invasion of Russia in 1812.
After Prussia's defeat at Jena-Auerstedt in 1806, reformers such as Scharnhorst and Gneisenau reorganized the Prussian army.
Napoleon's Berlin Decree of 1806 began the Continental System, an attempt to block British trade with the continent.
The Congress of Vienna met in 1814-1815; leading figures included Metternich of Austria, Castlereagh of Britain, Tsar Alexander I of Russia and Talleyrand of France.
The settlement restored the Bourbon monarchy in France and aimed at a balance of power among the great powers.
The Quadruple Alliance of 1815 (Austria, Prussia, Russia, Britain) and the Holy Alliance of 1815 were meant to preserve the post-Napoleonic order.

a: Kant argues that standing armies threaten other states with war simply by being always ready to fight.
Kant claims standing armies cause an arms race in which states try to outdo one another in numbers of soldiers, with no limit.
Kant argues that the cost of keeping armies makes peace more burdensome than a short war, so states start aggressive wars to escape that cost.
Kant argues that paying men to kill or be killed treats them as machines or tools of the state, which conflicts with human dignity or rights.
b: The levee en masse of 1793 mobilized French men on a mass scale, and other states had to raise larger forces in response, which supports Kant's point that armies push rivals into an unlimited contest over numbers.
Napoleon's conscripted Grande Armee was used for repeated wars of conquest, such as the 1812 invasion of Russia, which supports Kant's claim that large standing forces lead to aggressive war.
After Jena in 1806, Prussian reformers such as Scharnhorst and Gneisenau rebuilt the army so Prussia could match France, showing the competition in military strength Kant described.

The citizen armies of revolutionary France complicate Kant's argument, because they were raised from the nation for the war rather than hired as a permanent professional force, and they were still used for expansion.
c: Difference: the Vienna settlement kept the peace through a balance of power among great powers that still had large armies, instead of abolishing standing armies as Kant proposed.
Difference: the peacemakers of 1815 restored legitimate monarchs such as the Bourbons and redrew borders by great-power bargaining, rather than resting peace on principles of right as Kant hoped.
Similarity: like Kant, the powers at Vienna wanted a lasting peace rather than a short truce, and they set up regular cooperation through the Quadruple Alliance and the Concert of Europe.
Difference: the Quadruple and Holy Alliances were prepared to use military force against revolution, while Kant saw armies themselves as a cause of war.

common_pitfalls: Saying Kant is describing the Napoleonic Wars; the essay is a proposal from 1795 and came before Napoleon took power.
In part B, naming an event without explaining how it relates to Kant's argument about standing armies.
Using events outside 1789-1815, or the partitions of Poland, in parts B or C.
Treating the Congress of Vienna as a disarmament agreement.
Claiming that Kant wrote in response to one specific battle, or that he saw the wars at first hand.
contextualization_ideas: Enlightenment thinkers' criticism of dynastic wars and the cost of permanent armies under absolute monarchs.
The wars of the First Coalition against revolutionary France, from 1792.
The Peace of Basel of 1795 between Prussia and France, the same year Kant published the essay.
outside_evidence: Levee en masse, 1793
Napoleonic conscription and the Grande Armee
Prussian military reforms after Jena, 1806
Continental System, 1806
Congress of Vienna and Treaties of Paris, 1814-1815
Quadruple Alliance and Holy Alliance, 1815

doc_uses.usable_for: Enlightenment arguments about the causes of war and the moral cost of standing armies
doc_uses.sourcing: A Prussian philosopher writing a theoretical proposal for peace in 1795, while the revolutionary wars were going on and in the year Prussia made peace with France; it is a normative argument, not a report of events.

input.title: Religious Conflict and State Authority in Europe, c. 1450 to c. 1789

prompt.scenario: Between the fifteenth and the late eighteenth centuries, Europe went from a Latin Christendom under a single church to a continent split among Catholic, Lutheran, Reformed, Anglican and other confessions. In the same centuries, monarchs and other governments claimed more and more power over religion, and some of them later turned to policies of limited toleration.
prompt.task: Evaluate the extent to which religious change and religious conflict transformed the relationship between religious authority and political authority in Europe from c. 1450 to c. 1789. You are not expected to address the entire time period.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least two pieces of specific and relevant evidence.
Use historical reasoning (causation, comparison, or continuity and change) to frame or structure an argument that addresses the prompt.
Use evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument that addresses the prompt, demonstrating a complex understanding.

rows.task_specific: A claim that evaluates how far religious change and conflict transformed the relationship between church and state authority, c. 1450 to c. 1789. It should take a position on the extent of change, for example by pointing to state control over churches, the growth of confessional states, or later moves toward toleration, and should signal a line of reasoning.

descriptors.0: The response restates the prompt, has no defensible claim, or makes a claim with no line of reasoning about the extent of change in church-state relations.
descriptors.1: The response makes a historically defensible claim about how far religious authority and political authority were transformed and indicates the reasons or categories the argument will develop.

rows.task_specific: Relevant developments before or during the period that frame the argument. Examples include late medieval challenges to papal authority (the Avignon papacy, the Great Schism, conciliarism, Wycliffe and Hus), Renaissance humanism and the printing press, the growth of territorial monarchies, or Enlightenment criticism of religious persecution.

descriptors.0: The response gives no relevant context, or only a phrase or passing mention not tied to the argument.
descriptors.1: The response describes a broader historical development and explains how it relates to the changing relationship between religious and political authority.

rows.task_specific: Specific, accurate examples such as the Act of Supremacy (1534), the Peace of Augsburg (1555), the Edict of Nantes (1598) and its revocation (1685), the Peace of Westphalia (1648), the Dutch Revolt, the Toleration Act (1689), or Joseph II's Patent of Toleration (1781). One point goes for identifying relevant examples; the second requires that at least two of them be used to support the argument.

descriptors.0: The response gives no specific relevant evidence.
descriptors.1: The response gives at least two specific, accurate examples relevant to religion and political authority but does not use them to support an argument.
descriptors.2: The response uses at least two specific, accurate examples to support an argument about the extent of change in the relationship between religious and political authority.

rows.task_specific: Continuity and change (or causation or comparison) used to frame the argument, for example change from papal supremacy to state-controlled churches alongside continuity in the belief that religious unity guaranteed political order. Complex understanding might come from tracing both change and continuity across regions, comparing Protestant and Catholic states, explaining several causes, or qualifying the argument with counterevidence such as Catholic monarchs who gained church control without breaking with Rome.

descriptors.0: The response does not use historical reasoning to frame an argument about the prompt.
descriptors.1: The response uses continuity and change, causation, or comparison to frame or structure an argument about religious and political authority.
descriptors.2: The response shows a complex understanding, for example by weighing change against continuity, comparing different states, or using counterevidence to qualify or modify the argument.

scoring_notes: ALTON reference — not official AP scoring
Responses may concentrate on c. 1450 to c. 1648 or move into the eighteenth century. Full coverage of the span is not required, but the argument must address the extent of change.
Evidence may come from any part of Europe, including Poland-Lithuania, the Habsburg lands, Scandinavia, Iberia, and the British Isles.
A narrative of Reformation events without a judgment about how church-state relations changed should not earn the analysis points.
The complexity point is earned through sustained argument, not a single sentence that mentions another perspective.

defensible_theses: Religious conflict deeply changed the relationship between church and state: rulers in Protestant and Catholic lands alike took control of religious institutions. Yet until the late eighteenth century most governments still assumed that religious uniformity was necessary for political stability.

The Reformation and the religious wars moved authority over religion from the papacy to territorial rulers, as the Peace of Augsburg and the Peace of Westphalia show. After 1648, exhaustion from war and Enlightenment ideas pushed some states toward limited toleration. That toleration was granted by the state, not won as a right.

The change was more limited than it first appears. Many Catholic monarchs, such as Francis I through the Concordat of Bologna, had already gained great control over the church before the Reformation. Confessional persecution continued long after 1648, as Louis XIV's revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 shows.
contextualization_ideas: Late medieval challenges to papal authority, including the Avignon papacy, the Great Schism, the conciliar movement, and the reform movements of John Wycliffe and Jan Hus, had already weakened papal prestige before 1517.
The printing press and Christian humanism, such as Erasmus's work on the Greek New Testament, spread criticism of clerical abuses and made religious debate available to a wider public.
The growth of New Monarchies in France, England, and Spain, and the fragmented political structure of the Holy Roman Empire, shaped how rulers could use religious change to increase their own power.
outside_evidence: Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses (1517) and his appearance at the Diet of Worms (1521) depended on protection from Frederick the Wise of Saxony, which showed how princes could shelter religious reform.
Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy (1534) made the English monarch head of the Church of England, and the dissolution of the monasteries (1536 to 1541) moved church wealth to the crown.
The Peace of Augsburg (1555) let each prince of the Holy Roman Empire choose between Lutheranism and Catholicism for his territory, a principle later summarized as cuius regio, eius religio.

The French Wars of Religion, including the St. Bartholomew's Day Massacre (1572), ended with Henry IV's Edict of Nantes (1598), which granted Huguenots limited toleration. Louis XIV revoked it with the Edict of Fontainebleau (1685).
The Dutch Revolt against Philip II of Spain combined religious grievances with political ones. It led to the Union of Utrecht (1579) and the Act of Abjuration (1581).
The Council of Trent (1545 to 1563) and the Jesuit order (approved in 1540) strengthened Catholic doctrine and education, often in alliance with Catholic rulers such as the Habsburgs.

The Thirty Years' War (1618 to 1648) began with the Defenestration of Prague. Cardinal Richelieu's Catholic France supported Protestant Sweden against the Habsburgs. The Peace of Westphalia (1648) recognized Calvinism and confirmed the princes' authority over religion in their territories.
The Warsaw Confederation (1573) in Poland-Lithuania guaranteed religious peace among the nobility.
The Spanish Inquisition (established in 1478) and the expulsion of Jews from Spain (1492) show monarchs enforcing religious unity as a policy of state.

The Glorious Revolution (1688 to 1689) and the Toleration Act (1689) gave Protestant Dissenters in England freedom of worship but kept Catholics and Dissenters out of full political rights. John Locke's Letter Concerning Toleration (1689) argued for separating religious belief from civil government.

Voltaire campaigned over the Calas affair (1762) and wrote the Treatise on Tolerance (1763). Joseph II's Patent of Toleration (1781) and France's Edict of Versailles (1787) reflected Enlightenment-era toleration granted by the state.
Portugal (1759), France (1764), and Spain (1767) expelled the Jesuits, and Pope Clement XIV suppressed the order in 1773. This shows Catholic monarchs placing the church under state interests.
common_pitfalls: Writing a narrative of the Reformation without judging how far relations between church and state changed.
Assuming that religious toleration began in 1648, or ignoring persecution after Westphalia, such as the revocation of the Edict of Nantes.
Treating only Protestant states as gaining control over churches, while ignoring Catholic examples such as the Concordat of Bologna or the expulsions of the Jesuits.
Mixing up the Peace of Augsburg, which covered only Lutherans and Catholics, with the Peace of Westphalia, which added Calvinists.
Reducing every religious war to a single cause instead of recognizing that dynastic, political, and religious motives were combined.
Moving into United States history, such as the First Amendment, instead of keeping the focus on Europe.
facts: Luther posted the Ninety-five Theses in 1517.
The English Act of Supremacy was passed in 1534.
The Peace of Augsburg was concluded in 1555.
The Council of Trent met from 1545 to 1563.
Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes in 1598, and Louis XIV revoked it in 1685.
The Thirty Years' War lasted from 1618 to 1648 and ended with the Peace of Westphalia.
The English Toleration Act was passed in 1689.
Joseph II issued the Patent of Toleration in 1781.
The Concordat of Bologna (1516) gave the French king the right to nominate bishops and abbots.

input.title: SAQ 3: A U.S. Tank at Checkpoint Charlie, Berlin, 1961

prompt.scenario: In the period c. 1945 to 1991, Berlin was a divided city where the United States and the Soviet Union faced each other directly. In 1961, tensions over the city's future came to a head. This photograph was taken that year by a U.S. Army photographer at a crossing point between the American sector of West Berlin and East Berlin.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE feature of the photograph that shows the military character of the division of Berlin in 1961.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE specific historical development in the period 1945 to 1961, not shown in the photograph, that helps explain why United States forces were present at a crossing point between West Berlin and East Berlin in 1961.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE way the Cold War division of Europe between the Soviet-led and United States-led blocs affected a country in Central or Eastern Europe other than Germany in the period 1945 to 1991.

requirements: Each part asks for ONE item and is scored separately at 0 or 1 point.
Part A must rely on what can actually be seen in the photograph.
Part B must use a development from 1945 to 1961 that is not simply a description of the photograph.
Part C must name a specific country in Central or Eastern Europe other than Germany and a specific situation from 1945 to 1991.

rows.task_specific: Describe one visible feature of the image that shows the division as militarized, such as the U.S. Army tank with a white star and crew in its hatches, its position at the edge of the crossing, uniformed men standing on the far side, the barrier gate, or the painted line on the road.

descriptors.0: The response names no visible feature, describes something that cannot be seen, or makes claims about the unreadable sign's words.
descriptors.1: The response accurately describes one visible feature of the photograph and connects it to the armed or guarded nature of the Berlin division.

rows.task_specific: Explain one development from 1945 to 1961 that accounts for the American military presence at the sector boundary, such as four-power occupation after 1945, the Berlin Blockade and Airlift, the founding of two German states in 1949, Khrushchev's demands over Berlin from 1958, the flight of East Germans through West Berlin, or the building of the Wall in August 1961.

descriptors.0: The response gives no development, uses one outside 1945 to 1961, only restates the photograph, or gives an inaccurate development.
descriptors.1: The response explains one accurate, specific development from 1945 to 1961 and shows how it helps explain why U.S. forces stood at a Berlin crossing point in 1961.

rows.task_specific: Explain one specific effect of bloc division on a named Central or Eastern European country other than Germany, such as Soviet suppression of the Hungarian uprising in 1956, the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968, Communist takeovers after 1945, Warsaw Pact membership, or the end of Communist rule in 1989.

descriptors.0: The response names no country, picks Germany, stays general, or gives inaccurate history.
descriptors.1: The response explains one accurate, specific way the bloc division affected a named country in Central or Eastern Europe other than Germany between 1945 and 1991.

scoring_notes: ALTON reference — not official AP scoring
Each part earns 0 or 1 point; responses do not need full sentences of thesis quality but must do more than list a term.
Do not reward claims about the wording on the sign in the photograph, which cannot be read.

The exact date of the photograph is uncertain beyond the year 1961. Do not require students to say it shows the October 1961 tank standoff, and do not penalize a student who mentions that standoff as related context, provided the response does not claim the photograph definitely shows it.
For Part B, the building of the Berlin Wall in August 1961 is acceptable because the photograph does not show the Wall.

common_pitfalls: Inventing the words on the sign or saying what it advertises.
Stating as fact that the photograph shows the October 1961 standoff with Soviet tanks, when its exact date is unknown.
Claiming the uniformed men are Soviet soldiers when the image does not make their identity clear.
For Part B, only describing the tank again instead of explaining an earlier development.
For Part C, choosing East Germany or Berlin, or writing about the Cuban Missile Crisis, which is not a Central or Eastern European country.
Mixing up dates, for example putting the Berlin Airlift in 1961 or the fall of the Wall in 1991.
facts: After the Second World War, Germany and Berlin were split into four occupation zones and sectors run by the United States, Britain, France and the Soviet Union.
The Soviet blockade of West Berlin in 1948 to 1949 was answered by the Western Berlin Airlift.
The Federal Republic of Germany and the German Democratic Republic were both founded in 1949.
NATO was founded in 1949 and the Warsaw Pact in 1955.
In 1958 Khrushchev demanded that the Western powers leave West Berlin and that it become a demilitarized free city.
Kennedy and Khrushchev met at the Vienna summit in June 1961 and did not settle the Berlin question.
Millions of East Germans left for the West before 1961, many by way of West Berlin.
East German authorities began building the Berlin Wall on 13 August 1961.
In late October 1961, U.S. and Soviet tanks faced each other at Checkpoint Charlie after a dispute over Allied access to East Berlin.
The Berlin Wall was opened on 9 November 1989.

a: A U.S. Army tank marked with a white star sits right at the crossing, with crew members visible in its hatches, which shows armed forces guarding the sector line.
Several uniformed men stand on the far side of the crossing, so both sides of the boundary are watched by men in uniform.
A barrier gate and a painted line across the road mark the crossing as a controlled border inside a single city.
The size of the tank, with its long gun and front blade, compared with the ordinary street and parked van shows how a city street had been turned into a military frontier.
b: After 1945 the Allies divided Berlin into four sectors, which gave the United States a legal right to keep troops in its sector of West Berlin.
The Soviet blockade of West Berlin in 1948 to 1949 and the Western airlift made the defense of West Berlin a test of American commitment in Europe.
From 1958 Khrushchev demanded that the Western powers leave West Berlin, and the Vienna summit of June 1961 left the dispute unsolved, so U.S. forces stayed to show they would not withdraw.

The flight of millions of East Germans through West Berlin led East German authorities to begin the Berlin Wall in August 1961, turning the sector boundary into a fortified border that U.S. forces watched closely.
c: In Hungary in 1956, Soviet troops crushed an uprising after Imre Nagy's government announced it would leave the Warsaw Pact, showing that the Soviet Union would use force to keep its bloc together.
In Czechoslovakia in 1968, Warsaw Pact forces invaded to end the Prague Spring reforms of Alexander Dubcek.
In Poland in the late 1940s, Communists backed by the Soviet Union took power, and the country joined the Warsaw Pact in 1955, placing it inside the Soviet bloc.
In Poland in 1989, partly free elections brought Solidarity into government, an early step in the collapse of Communist rule across Eastern Europe as Soviet control weakened.

contextualization_ideas: Wartime alliance breaking down into the Cold War after 1945.
West Berlin as a Western enclave deep inside East German territory.
outside_evidence: Berlin Airlift 1948 to 1949
Construction of the Berlin Wall, August 1961
October 1961 tank standoff at Checkpoint Charlie
Kennedy's Berlin speech of June 1963
Opening of the Wall, November 1989
reasoning_types: Sourcing and describing a visual source

doc_uses.usable_for: Showing the militarized American presence at a Berlin sector crossing in 1961
doc_uses.sourcing: A U.S. Army photograph, so it was made by one side of the confrontation; the view from above stresses the size of the American tank. Its exact date within 1961 is uncertain.

input.title: Ideas, Movements, and the Position of Women in Europe, 1762 to 1914

prompt.scenario: Between the publication of Rousseau's Emile in 1762 and the outbreak of the First World War in 1914, European writers argued about women's nature, education, and rights, and by the late nineteenth century organized movements were campaigning for women's political rights, above all the parliamentary vote. Laws on marriage, property, education, and the franchise changed in some places and stayed fixed in others.
prompt.task: Evaluate the extent to which ideas and political movements changed the legal and social position of women in Europe between 1762 and 1914.
requirements: Respond to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.
Describe a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.
Support an argument in response to the prompt using at least four documents.
Use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence (beyond that found in the documents) relevant to an argument about the prompt.
For at least two documents, explain how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to an argument.
Use evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument that addresses the prompt.

rows.task_specific: A defensible claim about how far ideas and movements changed women's legal and social position from 1762 to 1914, with a line of reasoning, for example that arguments for equality spread widely and produced organized mass campaigns, but legal gains stayed partial and most European women still could not vote in national elections by 1914.

descriptors.0: Restates the prompt, gives no defensible claim, or makes a claim with no line of reasoning about the extent of change.
descriptors.1: Makes a defensible claim about the extent of change that sets up a line of reasoning, located in the introduction or conclusion.

rows.task_specific: Describes a broader development relevant to the prompt, such as Enlightenment debates on natural rights, the French Revolution and the Napoleonic Code, industrialization and the ideology of separate spheres, the expansion of the male franchise in the nineteenth century, or the growth of socialism and mass politics.

descriptors.0: Gives no relevant context or only a passing phrase.
descriptors.1: Describes a broader historical development and connects it to the question of women's legal and social position.

rows.task_specific: Uses document content to address the prompt: for example Rousseau's defense of female subjection, Wollstonecraft's and Mill's arguments for reason and equality, Engels's tie between women's oppression and class, and the suffrage poster, Fawcett, and Pankhurst as evidence of organized campaigning and its limits.

descriptors.0: Uses fewer than three documents accurately, or only quotes or summarizes them.
descriptors.1: Accurately describes content from at least three documents that relates to the topic.
descriptors.2: Supports an argument about the prompt with accurate content from at least four documents.

rows.task_specific: Uses specific evidence not found in the documents, such as the Napoleonic Code of 1804, the British Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882, the defeat of Mill's 1867 amendment, the Finnish grant of the vote to women in 1906, or suffragette hunger strikes and force-feeding.

descriptors.0: Gives no outside evidence, or gives evidence that is vague, inaccurate, or unrelated to an argument.
descriptors.1: Uses at least one specific, accurate piece of outside evidence and explains how it relates to an argument.

rows.task_specific: Explains how point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience matters for at least two documents, for example Fawcett's position as president of the peaceful NUWSS, Pankhurst's position as WSPU founder writing an autobiography in 1914, the persuasive aim of a poster made for a suffrage organization, or Engels writing as a German socialist in 1884.

descriptors.0: Does not source documents, or only names the author or date without explaining why that matters.
descriptors.1: Explains for at least two documents how point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience matters for an argument.

rows.task_specific: Shows a complex understanding, for example by weighing intellectual change against limited legal change, by contrasting constitutional and militant strategies, by setting liberal feminism beside socialist analysis, or by comparing British outcomes with other European cases.

descriptors.0: Does not show a complex understanding, or mentions complexity only in a phrase.
descriptors.1: Builds a complex understanding through sustained analysis, such as weighing several causes or explaining both change and continuity, or through sourcing of most documents tied to the argument.

scoring_notes: ALTON reference — not official AP scoring
The thesis may argue for substantial, moderate, or limited change; credit any defensible claim that is supported by the essay.
Documents 1 and 2 are dated 1762 and 1792; students may use them as background to the nineteenth century but should not treat Rousseau's view as unchallenged by 1914 or as a law.
Treat Document 5 as a persuasive image; credit readings of the uneven scales as a claim that women were treated unjustly, but do not require any particular identification of the hooded figure.
Outside evidence after 1914, such as the British Representation of the People Act of 1918, may support an argument about limits before 1914 but must be framed accurately.

defensible_theses: Between 1762 and 1914, writers such as Wollstonecraft and Mill turned the assumption of natural female subjection into a contested political question, and later movements turned that argument into mass organizing; even so, the legal change that followed was partial. By 1914 married women in Britain had gained property rights, but most European women still had no national vote.

Organized political movements did more than abstract ideas to change women's position. The NUWSS network of more than 300 societies and the militant WSPU made women's rights a public issue that governments could not ignore, though their arguments over tactics also show how hard it was to win the parliamentary vote.

Ideas and movements changed women's social and educational position more than their legal standing. Liberal and socialist critiques reached wide audiences and women entered public campaigning, but as Mill predicted, ideas about women rooted in feeling outlasted the arguments against them. Rousseau's model of separate roles survived in law codes and political practice until 1914.
contextualization_ideas: Enlightenment natural rights thought and the French Revolution raised claims of universal rights. Olympe de Gouges and Wollstonecraft applied those claims to women, but the revolutionaries closed women's political clubs in 1793 and the Napoleonic Code of 1804 placed wives under their husbands' authority.

Industrialization and the growth of the middle class strengthened the ideology of separate spheres, which assigned women to the home. At the same time, women's factory work led to protective laws such as the Mines Act of 1842.

Over the nineteenth century the male franchise expanded through the Reform Acts of 1832, 1867, and 1884, and mass politics and socialism grew. Women's exclusion from the vote therefore became more visible and more organized movements formed to challenge it.
outside_evidence: Olympe de Gouges published the Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen in 1791 and was executed in 1793.
In 1793 the French revolutionary government banned women's political clubs.
The Napoleonic Code of 1804 required a wife to obey her husband and limited married women's control of property.
The Matrimonial Causes Act of 1857 created civil divorce courts in England.
In 1867 Mill proposed an amendment to the Second Reform Bill replacing the word man with person, and the House of Commons defeated it.
The Married Women's Property Acts of 1870 and 1882 let married women in Britain keep their own earnings and property.
Josephine Butler led the campaign against the Contagious Diseases Acts, which were repealed in 1886.
Girton College, Cambridge, was founded for women in 1869.

August Bebel's Woman and Socialism, published in 1879, linked women's emancipation to socialist revolution. In 1910 Clara Zetkin proposed an International Women's Day at a socialist women's conference in Copenhagen.
Finland gave women the national vote in 1906 and Norway did so in 1913.
Imprisoned suffragettes went on hunger strike and were force-fed from 1909, and the Cat and Mouse Act of 1913 allowed hunger strikers to be released and then rearrested.
Emily Wilding Davison died after running onto the course at the 1913 Derby.

doc_uses.usable_for: Evidence of the eighteenth-century view that women were made to please men and be in subjection to them, which later reformers challenged and which helps explain how far change had to go.
doc_uses.sourcing: Rousseau wrote this in a 1762 book on education, so his claims about women are part of an educational program that rests on assumptions about nature. As a famous Enlightenment writer, his view carried influence, which is why later writers felt they had to answer it.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows an Enlightenment-based argument that women should be educated to use their own reason and have power over themselves, a direct challenge to Rousseau.
doc_uses.sourcing: Wollstonecraft published in 1792, during the French Revolution and its debates over rights. Because she was answering Rousseau directly, the excerpt shows ideas about women being argued over in print. Students should note that the quoted words are her rendering of Rousseau's argument.

doc_uses.usable_for: States a liberal case that the legal subordination of women is wrong and should give way to perfect equality. It also concedes that opinions rooted in feeling resist argument, which helps explain why change was limited.
doc_uses.sourcing: Mill had been a member of Parliament from 1865 to 1868 and published the book in 1869, so he wrote with direct political experience at a time when the franchise was being debated. His standing as a well-known philosopher gave the argument a wide hearing.

doc_uses.usable_for: Presents a socialist explanation that ties women's oppression to private property and class, suggesting that legal reform alone would not end it.
doc_uses.sourcing: Engels was a German socialist who published this in 1884, the year after Marx died, and he cites a manuscript he wrote with Marx. His purpose is to fit the family into a Marxist account of history, which shapes his emphasis on class over legal rights.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows that by 1909 organized suffragists were making a mass visual appeal that framed the vote as a matter of justice, with the uneven scales suggesting unequal treatment. It is also evidence that women still lacked the vote.
doc_uses.sourcing: Mary Lowndes designed the poster for a British women's suffrage organization, so it was made to persuade the public and is advocacy, not neutral description. The 1909 date places it during the most intense phase of the British campaign.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows the rapid growth of organized constitutional suffrage societies, which numbered 305 by October 1911, and claims that the movement combined order with audacity.
doc_uses.sourcing: As president of the NUWSS, which used peaceful methods, Fawcett had reason to stress her organization's size and success. Writing in 1912, before the vote was won, she also had reason to present the movement as respectable and growing.

doc_uses.usable_for: Shows the founding of a women-only, militant organization with the motto Deeds, not words, and its frustration with older leaders and with politicians. This is evidence of division within the movement and of limited legislative results.
doc_uses.sourcing: Pankhurst founded the WSPU in 1903 and published this autobiography in 1914, so she was justifying her own militant strategy. That purpose explains her dismissive picture of the older constitutional leaders and of hypocritical politicians.

evidence_map.line: Enlightenment, liberal, and socialist ideas mounted a growing intellectual challenge to the assumption that women were naturally subordinate.
Organized political movements turned arguments for equality into mass public campaigns that changed women's role in public life.
The legal position of women, especially on the vote, changed only to a limited extent by 1914 because entrenched beliefs and politicians resisted reform.
Reformers disagreed about the causes of women's subordination and how to end it, which shaped and sometimes divided the movements.

common_pitfalls: Claiming that British women won the parliamentary vote before 1914, or ignoring that the British vote came only in 1918 and then with limits.
Treating Rousseau's view as a law or as the only opinion of his era.
Summarizing each document in turn without arguing about the extent of change.
Discussing only the suffrage campaign and ignoring property, marriage, education, and work.
Describing the image in detail without connecting it to an argument, or reading meanings into it that the image does not support.
Using United States suffrage history in place of European evidence.
Sourcing by naming the author only, without explaining how position or purpose affects the document.
facts: Rousseau published Emile in 1762.
Wollstonecraft published A Vindication of the Rights of Woman in 1792.
Mill was a member of Parliament from 1865 to 1868 and published The Subjection of Women in 1869.
Engels published The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State in 1884, after Marx's death in 1883.
Mary Lowndes designed the Justice demands the vote poster in 1909 for the Artists' Suffrage League.
Fawcett led the NUWSS, which used constitutional methods, and published her history in 1912.
Emmeline Pankhurst founded the WSPU in Manchester in 1903 and published My Own Story in 1914.
Finland in 1906 and Norway in 1913 gave women the national vote; Britain did so in 1918, for women over 30 who met property qualifications.

input.title: Columbus on Española, 1493: Iberian Exploration and the Beginnings of Atlantic Empire

prompt.scenario: In the period c. 1450 to c. 1600, Portuguese and Spanish voyages backed by their monarchs laid the foundations of the first European Atlantic empires. In 1493 Christopher Columbus, an Italian-born navigator sailing for the Spanish crown, wrote a letter on the voyage home from his first Atlantic crossing.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Briefly describe ONE claim Columbus makes in the excerpt about Española or about what the Spanish crown could gain from it.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE development in Portuguese or Spanish exploration or royal policy in the period 1450 to 1500 that helps explain the goals Columbus expresses in the excerpt. Do not use the excerpt's own details as your development.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Briefly explain ONE effect of Spanish colonization of the Americas in the period 1492 to 1600 on either the Indigenous peoples of the Americas or on Spain and the rest of Europe.

requirements: Each part asks for ONE item and is scored separately.
Part B must use a specific development from 1450 to 1500 that is not taken from the excerpt.
Part C must use a specific effect from 1492 to 1600 tied to the Indigenous peoples of the Americas or to Spain and Europe.

rows.task_specific: The response correctly describes a claim from the excerpt, such as that Española has rich land for farming, raising cattle and building towns; that its rivers carry gold; that Columbus has taken possession of the islands for the Spanish monarchs so they can rule them as fully as Castile; or that a town on Española is well placed for gold mining and for trade, including trade with the land of the great Khan.

descriptors.0: The response does not describe a claim actually made in the excerpt, or it only quotes the text without saying what Columbus claims.
descriptors.1: The response accurately describes one claim Columbus makes about Española or about what the crown could gain from it.

rows.task_specific: The response explains a specific Portuguese or Spanish development from 1450 to 1500 and connects it to Columbus's goals of gold, trade with Asia or claiming land for the crown. Good examples are Portuguese voyages along the African coast and the gold trade at Elmina, Dias rounding the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, the agreement Ferdinand and Isabella made with Columbus in 1492 after the conquest of Granada, or the race with Portugal that led to the Treaty of Tordesillas.

descriptors.0: The response names no accurate development from the stated years, gives only details from the excerpt, or does not connect the development to Columbus's goals.
descriptors.1: The response explains one accurate Portuguese or Spanish development from 1450 to 1500 and how it helps explain the goals Columbus expresses.

rows.task_specific: The response explains a specific effect of Spanish colonization between 1492 and 1600, either on Indigenous peoples (epidemic disease and population collapse, the encomienda system of forced labor, religious conversion by missionaries) or on Spain and Europe (silver from Potosí and Mexico, rising prices, new crops such as maize and potatoes from the Columbian exchange, the start of the transatlantic slave trade to the Americas).

descriptors.0: The response gives no accurate effect from the stated years, gives an effect with no link to Spanish colonization, or only repeats the excerpt.
descriptors.1: The response explains one accurate effect of Spanish colonization from 1492 to 1600 on Indigenous peoples of the Americas or on Spain and Europe.

scoring_notes: ALTON reference — not official AP scoring
Score each part on its own; a strong answer to one part does not make up for a missing answer to another.
Part A requires reading the excerpt; general statements about exploration that are not in the text do not earn the point.

For Part B, the fall of Constantinople and Ottoman control of trade routes fall outside what this question asks, which is Portuguese or Spanish exploration or royal policy, so they do not earn the point by themselves.

The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) may earn credit in Part B as part of Iberian royal rivalry over newly claimed lands, or in Part C as an effect on how Europe divided its claims, as long as the response explains the link.
Do not credit statements that treat Columbus's descriptions of wealth as reliable fact; responses can describe them as his claims.

a: Columbus claims that Española's mountains, plains and fields are rich enough for planting crops, raising cattle and building towns, which presents the island as good land for settlement.
Columbus claims that most of Española's rivers carry gold, suggesting the island could make the crown rich.
Columbus states that he has taken possession of the islands for Ferdinand and Isabella and that they can control them as completely as they control the kingdom of Castile.

Columbus claims a town on Española is well placed for gold mining and for trade, including a hoped-for profitable trade with the land of the great Khan, which shows he believed he had reached the edge of Asia.
b: During the fifteenth century Portuguese voyages backed by Prince Henry and later kings worked their way down the West African coast, and Portugal's fort at Elmina (built 1482) gave it access to African gold. This success showed Castile that sea voyages could bring in gold and trade, which explains why Columbus stresses gold and commerce.

In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope, which opened an eastern sea route toward Asia for Portugal. Spain was competing for its own route to Asian trade, which explains why Columbus points to future commerce with the land of the great Khan.

In 1492, just after their conquest of Granada, Ferdinand and Isabella agreed to sponsor Columbus and promised him titles and a share of profits from the lands he found. As a crown-sponsored agent he had reason to stress claims of possession and wealth for 'their Highnesses.'

Rivalry with Portugal over newly found lands pushed the Spanish monarchs to secure their claims quickly, first through papal bulls in 1493 and then through the Treaty of Tordesillas in 1494. This helps explain Columbus's emphasis on formally taking possession for the crown.
c: Diseases carried by Europeans, such as smallpox, killed huge numbers of Indigenous people across the Caribbean and the mainland, and the Taíno population of Española collapsed within a few decades of contact.
Spain set up the encomienda system, which gave colonists the right to Indigenous labor and tribute. It led to forced labor and abuse that critics such as Bartolomé de las Casas condemned.
After 1545 large amounts of silver from Potosí and from Mexican mines flowed to Spain, paying for Habsburg wars and contributing to rising prices in Europe during the sixteenth century.
Through the Columbian exchange, American crops such as maize and potatoes spread to Europe, while Europeans brought horses, wheat and sugar cultivation to the Americas.

facts: Columbus's first voyage left Spain in August 1492 and reached the Caribbean in October 1492; he wrote this letter on the voyage home in early 1493.
Ferdinand of Aragon and Isabella of Castile sponsored the voyage; Granada fell to them in January 1492.
Portugal built the fort of São Jorge da Mina (Elmina) on the Gold Coast in 1482.
Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488; Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498.
The Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) between Spain and Portugal set a dividing line 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands.
Pedro Álvares Cabral reached Brazil in 1500, which Portugal claimed under the Tordesillas line.
The Potosí silver deposits were discovered in 1545.
Columbus believed he had reached islands off Asia; the excerpt's reference to the great Khan reflects that belief.
common_pitfalls: Using the fall of Constantinople or Ottoman control of trade routes as the Part B development, which this question does not ask for.
Repeating the excerpt's gold or fertile land as the Part B development instead of naming a separate historical development.
Treating Columbus's claims of great wealth as accurate rather than as promotional statements to his royal sponsors.
Saying Columbus knew he had found a new continent; the excerpt shows he thought he was near the land of the great Khan in Asia.
Giving a Part C effect from outside 1492 to 1600, or one about English or French colonies in North America that has nothing to do with Spanish colonization.
Naming an effect without explaining how it changed life for Indigenous peoples or for Spain and Europe.
contextualization_ideas: Iberian monarchies that had recently been centralized, and Castile in particular after the Reconquista, looked overseas for wealth and prestige.
Portuguese progress in navigation, including the caravel and better use of compass and astrolabe, made long Atlantic voyages possible.
Christian missionary aims and the papal role in granting claims shaped how Iberian rulers justified possession.

doc_uses.usable_for: Evidence of Spanish goals in the first voyage: claiming land for the crown, gold, settlement and trade with Asia.
doc_uses.sourcing: Written by a crown-sponsored navigator on his way home, so it has reason to play up the islands' wealth to justify the voyage and win support for more voyages; it was printed widely soon after. Read in the 1847 Major English translation.
